title: Phenological Shifts in the Ruby-Throated Hummingbird and its Preferred Flowers
text:
Introduction
With warming temperatures due to anthropogenic climate change, bird migration times are shifting, and they are tending to migrate back to their breeding grounds earlier each year. Along with this, flowers that certain migrating birds, like Ruby-throated Hummingbirds (Archilochus colubris), feed on may be changing the time of their first bloom due to climate change.



Ruby-throated Hummingbird


I want to investigate how a pollinating bird species, the Ruby-throated Hummingbird, has been shifting its migration patterns and how the appearances of two spring ephemeral species it prefers to feed on, Red Buckeye (Aesculus pavia) and Red Columbine (Aquilegia canadensis), has changed (or not changed) over the past *10 years.
*My maps and graphs are from 2014 to 2025 to account for any incomplete datasets from 2025



Red Columbine





Red Buckeye


I predict that Ruby-throated Hummingbirds are migrating back earlier each year, and they are arriving at higher latitudes increasingly earlier than lower latitudes. Additionally, I suppose that the first sightings of these preferred flowers in the months that Ruby-throated Hummingbirds migrate and settle back North will be earlier at higher latitudes and later at lower latitudes compared to previous years. So, as Ruby-throated Hummingbirds migrate back earlier, these flowers may not be available at lower latitudes for them to feed on.


Materials and methods

I installed leaflet and leaflet.extras for making maps, along with rinat and rnpn to download data from iNaturalist and the US National Phenology Network (NPN), respectively. I then loaded my necessary libraries. I used dplyr to mutate and filter data, lubridate to parse date data, and ggplot2 for plotting.

I combined the datasets from each year into one. Then, I saved this data into a csv so I do not have to download the data each time I run the code, and loaded it into my environment as “nat_flower”. I filtered nat_flower to only include wild sightings of the selected species (captive_cultivated = “false”).


#fl_all <- rbind(fl_2005, fl_2006, fl_2007, fl_2008, fl_2009, fl_2010, fl_2011, fl_2012, fl_2013, fl_2014, fl_2015, fl_2016, fl_2017, fl_2018, fl_2019, fl_2020, fl_2021, fl_2022, fl_2023, fl_2024, fl_2025)

#write.csv(fl_all, "data/fl_all.csv")

nat_flower <- read.csv("data/fl_all.csv")
nat_flower <- nat_flower %>%
  filter(captive_cultivated == "false")


I used the rnpn package to download data for the plant species from the NPN (which automatically saves as a csv). The species IDs were available through the NPN’s website (Red Buckeye = 784, columbine = 147).

# species_id=c(784, 147), 
# download_path="data/npn_flower.csv"
# )

npn_flower <- read.csv("data/npn_flower.csv")


I combined my iNaturalist and NPN data into one dataset.


all_flower <- nat_flower %>% full_join(npn_flower)

Joining with `by = join_by(latitude, longitude, common_name)`



I used the Lubridate package to standardize the format all of the dates in my flower data. Then, I used these standardized dates to create a year column, where I pulled the year from the dates, a year_day column, to transform the date into a day out of 365, and a month column to pull the month from the dates.


all_flower <- all_flower %>%
  mutate(observed_on = parse_date_time(observed_on, orders = c("mdy", "ydm", "dmy"))) %>%
  mutate(year = year(observed_on)) %>%
  mutate(year_day = yday(observed_on)) %>%
  mutate(month = month(observed_on))


I found the mean date of first sightings of the selected flowers from 2005 to 2013 and from March to June (when these flowers bloom; fl_early dataset) to compare data from the last 10 years. I separated sightings into 3 bands of latitude (to account for few observations and streamline, since there are similar sighting times for throughout these bands).


fl_early <- all_flower %>%
  filter(year %in% c(2005, 2006, 2007, 2008, 2009, 2010, 2011, 2012, 2013) & month %in% c(3, 4, 5, 6))

fl_early_30 <- fl_early %>%
  filter(latitude > 30 & latitude < 36) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE))

fl_early_36 <- fl_early %>%
  filter(latitude > 36 & latitude < 42) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE))

fl_early_42 <- fl_early %>%
  filter(latitude > 42 & latitude < 48) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE))

fl_early1 <- fl_early_30 %>% full_join(fl_early_36)
fl_early_all <- fl_early_42 %>% full_join(fl_early1)

#Checked each dataset for the mean bloom date


I created the dataset to see trends between 2014 and 2025, and in months March to June. I added a column (mean0013) with the means of the fl_early observations based on latitude. I used 6 bands of latitude, using 1 early mean for 2 bands here based on latitude. I also created a difference column, showing the difference in days of arrival between the 2014 and 2025 and the 2005 to 2013 average using mean - mean0013. I rejoined all of these bands into one dataset for plotting.


flower_new <- all_flower %>%
  filter(year %in% c(2014, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025) & month %in% c(3, 4, 5, 6)) %>%
  mutate(mean0013 = 
         case_when(
         latitude > 30 & latitude < 33 ~ 95.07143,
         latitude > 33 & latitude < 36 ~ 95.07143,
         latitude > 36 & latitude < 39 ~ 99.73333,
         latitude > 39 & latitude < 42 ~ 99.73333,
         latitude > 42 & latitude < 45 ~ 132.8696,
         latitude > 45 & latitude < 48 ~ 132.8696))

fl_30 <- flower_new %>%
  filter(latitude > 30 & latitude < 33) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(difference = mean - mean0013)

fl_33 <- flower_new %>%
  filter(latitude > 33 & latitude < 36) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(difference = mean - mean0013)

fl_36 <- flower_new %>%
  filter(latitude > 36 & latitude < 39) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(difference = mean - mean0013)

fl_39 <- flower_new %>%
  filter(latitude > 39 & latitude < 42) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(difference = mean - mean0013)

fl_42 <- flower_new %>%
  filter(latitude > 42 & latitude < 45) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(difference = mean - mean0013)

fl_45 <- flower_new %>%
  filter(latitude > 45 & latitude < 48) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(difference = mean - mean0013)

fl_1 <- fl_30 %>% full_join(fl_33)
fl_2 <- fl_36 %>% full_join(fl_39)
fl_3 <- fl_42 %>% full_join(fl_45)

fl_4 <- fl_1 %>% full_join(fl_2)

fl_new_all <- fl_3 %>%
  full_join(fl_4)

To download the Ruby-throated Hummingbird data from eBird on your own, visit: https://media.ebird.org/catalog?birdOnly=true&taxonCode=rthhum, filter by year (I did this in two separate actions [1995-2021 and 2022-2025] to ensure I could download all of the data), filter by location (United States), and download as a csv.

Parsing, mutating, and filtering Ruby-throat data based on their migration timeframe of February to May


ruby_throat <- rth_all %>%
  mutate(date_new = parse_date_time(Date, orders = c("mdy", "ydm", "dmy"))) %>%
  mutate(year_new = year(date_new)) %>%
  mutate(year_day = yday(date_new))

rth_early <- ruby_throat %>%
  filter(Year %in% c(2005, 2006, 2007, 2008, 2009, 2010, 2011, 2012, 2013) & Month %in% c(2,3,4,5))


Here is my code for finding the early Ruby-throat arrival dates. These bands are further filtered by month to account for their usual arrival times based on Courter et al., 2013 and Journey North:


rthearly30 <- rth_early %>%
  filter(Month %in% c(2,3)) %>%
  filter(Latitude > 29 & Latitude < 33) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE))

rthearly33 <- rth_early %>%
  filter(Month %in% c(3,4)) %>%
  filter(Latitude > 33 & Latitude < 36) %>%

rthearly36 <- rth_early %>%
  filter(Month %in% c(3,4)) %>%

rthearly39 <- rth_early %>%
  filter(Month %in% c(4,5)) %>%
  filter(Latitude > 39 & Latitude < 42) %>%

rthearly42 <- rth_early %>%
  filter(Month %in% c(4,5)) %>%
  filter(Latitude > 42 & Latitude < 45) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE)) 


I similarly created the Ruby-throat dataset for 2014-2025. I combined these bands into one dataset, and created a difference column, showing the difference in days of arrival between the new dataset and the 2005 to 2013 average using mean - mean0013.


rth_new_all <- ruby_throat %>%
  filter(Year %in% c(2014, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025) & Month %in% c(2, 3, 4, 5)) %>%
  mutate(mean0013 = 
  case_when(Latitude > 30 & Latitude < 33 ~ 77,
            Latitude > 33 & Latitude < 36 ~ 109.2778,
            Latitude > 36 & Latitude < 39 ~ 112.6667,
            Latitude > 39 & Latitude < 42 ~ 135.087,
            Latitude > 42 & Latitude < 45 ~ 141.75
                              ))                          
rth_30 <- rth_new_all %>%
  filter(Month %in% c(2,3)) %>%
  filter(Latitude > 30 & Latitude < 33) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(difference = mean - mean0013)

rth_33 <- rth_new_all %>%
  filter(Month %in% c(3,4)) %>%
  filter(Latitude > 33 & Latitude < 36) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(difference = mean - mean0013)

rth_36 <- rth_new_all %>%
  filter(Month %in% c(3,4)) %>%
  filter(Latitude > 36 & Latitude < 39) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(difference = mean - mean0013)

rth_39 <- rth_new_all %>%
  filter(Month %in% c(4,5)) %>%
  filter(Latitude > 39 & Latitude < 42) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(difference = mean - mean0013)

rth_42 <- rth_new_all %>%
  filter(Month %in% c(4,5)) %>%
  filter(Latitude > 42 & Latitude < 45) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(difference = mean - mean0013)

rth_1 <- rth_30 %>% full_join(rth_33)
rth_2 <- rth_36 %>% full_join(rth_39)
rth_3 <- rth_42 %>% full_join(rth_1)

rubythroat_all <- rth_2 %>% full_join(rth_3)


I created color palettes using viridis scales and colorNumeric from the Leaflet package for my two maps, specifying to use the difference column in each dataset to map the colors to.


cpal <- colorNumeric(palette = "viridis", domain = fl_new_all$difference, na.color = NA)

rpal <- colorNumeric(palette = "viridis", domain = rubythroat_all$difference, na.color = NA)

Assuming "longitude" and "latitude" are longitude and latitude, respectively









Conclusions
Trends for the preferred flowers have shown that its timing of first observations have changed from the 2005-2013 average. At the highest latitudes, there is a pattern of earlier sightings each year. But for latitudes between 30 and 39, flowers have been sighted later than in previous years. Since these flowers are spring ephemerals, warmer winter temperatures, or more extreme heat in spring and summer, may cause this trend, as these flowers will not bloom under extreme heat, or until they have gone through a period of sufficient cooling.
Similarly, the average first observation date for Ruby-throated hummingbirds has been generally shifting earlier with increasing latitudes.
These trends do somewhat align. All flower bloom times occur around or before the average date of Ruby-throat sightings. Ruby-throats thus may migrate back earlier, especially to higher latitudes, since their food is available earlier.
It is important to note, though, that this dataset is relatively small and data used to acquire average arrival/bloom dates for 2005 to 2013 was sparse. Additionally, since this data is collected from citizen science projects, the data may be more biased towards urban areas, and its distribution is not even. As shown in the heatmap for the flowers, observations do tend to be concentrated in urban areas. For Ruby-throats, the data was more plentiful for higher latitudes.
